Distinguished representative of state parties, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, good morning. On behalf of the Secretary General of the United Nations, I have the honor to open the 11th meeting of state parties to the Optional Protocol to the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, OPCAT. The High Commissioner for Human Rights, who is unable to open this meeting due to prior commitment, has asked me to convey to you his wishes for a successful meeting. Before turning to the first item on our agenda, allow me to share a few reflections on the implementation of the Optional Protocol to date. This year marks several important milestones, namely 20 years since the entry into force of the OPCAT, 20 years of the work of the Subcommittee on the Prevention of Torture, and 25 years since the adoption of the OPCAT by the General Assembly. Since its adoption, we have seen a gradual but steady increase in ratifications and accessions, bringing the number of State Parties to 96. I'm pleased to welcome to this meeting representatives of two States that have become party to the Optional Protocol since the last meeting. They are Bangladesh and Colombia. Excellencies, The Subcommittee has been very active since its establishment. It has undertaken 112 visits to State parties. This year, it has visited Mexico, France and Sri Lanka and will visit Paraguay and Ghana before the end of the year. During its visits, the Subcommittee, in addition to visiting places of deprivation of liberty, also works with the national preventive mechanisms where they are already in place. The SPT also conducts follow-up visits to States Parties to assess whether the recommendations from its prior visits have been implemented. Furthermore, 75 reports relating to countries and national preventive mechanisms across all regions have been made public at the request of States Parties or the national preventive mechanisms. reflecting the confidence placed in the SPT work. A key contribution of the OPCAT is the requirement for each State Party to maintain, designate or establish one or more independent national preventive mechanisms. To date, 80 out of the 96 State Parties have done so. As you know, The SPT supports States in establishing these mechanisms and ensuring their compliance with the Optional Protocol. It also maintains regular contact with national preventive mechanisms and the regional networks and provides advice upon request. Where appropriate, this advice is shared with the relevant States and mechanisms and made public. The SPT also collaborates with other mechanisms in the field of torture prevention, particularly the Committee against Torture, the Special Rapporteur on Torture, the Fund for Victims of Torture, and other international bodies. At the regional level, the SPT maintains close contacts with the Inter-American human rights system and the European Committee on the Prevention of Torture. Since the last meeting of State Parties, the SPT adopted a set of substantive documents providing technical advice, guidance on the follow-up to the subcommittees' visit procedures, as well as on issues of independence and impartiality in the context of the guidelines on the independence and impartiality of members of the human rights treaty bodies, also known as the Addis Ababa Guidelines. The subcommittee also provides or provided advice to national preventive mechanisms on remuneration of their experts, advice on national preventive mechanisms in multi-mandated institutions and on changes in the national preventive mechanisms designation. Finally, it also issued advice on the compliance of draft national legislation on national preventive mechanisms with the provisions of the Optional Protocol. Excellencies, I am pleased to inform you that the Chair of the SPT will present the 20th annual report of the SPT to the UN General Assembly on 15 October, together with the annual report of the Committee against Torture and the report of the Special Rapporteur on torture. Regrettably, the Chair of the SPT, like the Chairs of other treaty bodies, will join the meeting remotely as funds are not available to enable the travel to New York. Thanks to its unique and proactive approach, the SPT has become an essential reference point in the field of torture prevention. We should also underline the role played by civil society representatives in their ongoing support of the SPT and its core activities under the mandate of the OPCAT. Excellences, Madames and Messieurs.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I would also like to highlight the OPCAT Special Fund created under Article 26 of the Optional Protocol. These funds support the implementation of the recommendations of the OPCAT and shore up national prevention mechanisms. Since it was created, 161 projects have been funded by it in numerous countries to a total of $4 million. in the form of subsidies. Since 2016, the Fund has prioritised projects aimed at putting in place or strengthening national prevention mechanisms, placing an emphasis on achieving measurable, sustainable results, as well as strengthening the key roles of Member States in reforms. With voluntary contributions, the Special Fund depends on continued contributions from States, and I would like to sincerely thank those who have made their contributions, and I encourage others to do the same. Every contribution is a concrete demonstration of commitment in favour of preventing torture on the global scale. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this meeting comes at a time when we see considerable uncertainty and challenges where the United Nations system meets major restrictions to its operations. The liquidity crisis and partial release of funds through tranches has affected the ability that we have to plan Treaty Body visits as well as other operations. Visits require planning that is becoming more complicated due to the lack of persistent financial unpredictability. This is why the SPT has had to reduce our programme of visits in 2025 and in 2026, as well as our consultations to national prevention mechanisms. As we respond to the immediate difficulties that flow from the financial situation, we must also continue to think carefully about the ways that we could shore up in the long term the treaty bodies system. Allow me to draw your attention to the working document of the High Commission for Human Rights entitled "Strengthening the efficacy and efficiency of the treaty body systems of the United Nations". Commissioner's Office compiled this document to encourage a discussion on strengthening the treaty bodies. The sixth report of the Secretary General on the state of the treaty bodies, as well as its annexes, are available on the website, and I think that they will be of great interest to everyone. Finally, I would like to mention the election of an informal online session with the election candidates who have chosen to participate. This event has become a practice that is well established, organised by the Association for the Prevention of Torture and the consortium United Against Torture, with support from the Secretariat. Many participants, notably from State Parties and civil society, as well as the current SPT members, have participated in this event. Every candidate has prepared a brief oral presentation, which is followed by questions posed by Member States and other participants. This virtual meeting is much appreciated by the candidate state parties and other participants because it makes it possible to exchange allow exchanges between the candidates and the parties state parties who have chosen to elect them this event is also called upon to preserve diversity and inclusivity within the committee and across the treaty bodies the committee has set an example for gender balance with 13 men and 12 women in its current composition, as well as in terms of the diversity of skills and experience. And I encourage you to continue this positive trend during the upcoming election and subsequent elections.

Ladies and gentlemen, allow me to move to the elections. In this regard, I would like to reiterate the criteria set out in the Optional Protocol concerning members of and their professional qualification. Article 5 stipulates, in part, "The members of the subcommittee on prevention shall be chosen from among persons of high moral character, having proven professional experience in the field of the administration of justice, in particular in criminal law, prisons or police administration, or in the various fields relevant to the treatment of persons deprived of their liberty." 3. In the composition of the Subcommittee on Prevention, due consideration shall be given to equitable geographic distribution and to the representation of different forms of civilization and legal systems of the States Parties. 4. In this composition, consideration shall also be given to balanced gender representation on the basis of the principle of equality and non-discrimination. The members of the Sub-Committee on Prevention shall serve in their individual capacity, shall be independent and impartial, and shall be available to serve the Sub-Committee on Prevention efficiently. The SPT should therefore be composed of independent experts reflecting a variety of professional and personal skills to carry out its mandate effectively and independently. It should also be noted that the Subcommittee is guided by the principle of confidentiality, impartiality, non-selectivity, universality, and objectivity as set out in the Optional Protocol. Today, we will hold the election of 13 members of the Subcommittee to fill the vacant positions that will expire on 31 December 2026. In accordance with Article 15 of the Rules of Procedure, the 13 candidates who obtain in the first ballot the largest number of votes and an absolute majority of the votes of the representatives of States Parties present and voting will be elected. If the number of candidates obtaining such majority is less than 13, there shall be additional ballots to fill the remaining places. the voting being restricted to those candidates who obtained the largest number of votes in the previous ballot, and the number of candidates being limited to no more than twice the number of places remaining to be filled, with a provision that, after the third inconclusive ballot, votes may be cast for any eligible nominee. Still in accordance with Article 15, If two nationals of a State Party have become eligible to serve as members, the candidate receiving the higher number of votes shall serve as the member.
